emergency.general: Dial 112 for emergencies and ask for an ambulance. English is widely spoken in Tanzania alongside Swahili, but response times and service quality vary significantly outside major urban areas.

healthcare.summary: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to Tanzania. Emergency numbers (112/111/999), yellow fever requirements, pharmacy tips, restricted medications, malaria precautions, and travel insurance advice.

medications.prescriptionRules: A prescription is required for prescription medications but enforcement varies. Antibiotics and many drugs available OTC. Carry all medications in original packaging with a doctor's note.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD stimulant medications (Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse)
restrictedMeds.note: Stimulants are controlled substances. Bring original prescription, doctor's letter, and only the amount needed. Declare at customs.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine is controlled. Carry alternatives if possible.

restrictedMeds.name: Psychotropic medications (diazepam, alprazolam, etc.)
restrictedMeds.note: Benzodiazepines require documentation. Carry a doctor's letter explaining medical necessity.

restrictedMeds.name: Narcotics (morphine, tramadol, etc.)
restrictedMeds.note: Strong narcotics require strict documentation. Carry alternatives or minimal quantities with documentation.

medications.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. Yellow fever certificate required for entry if arriving from endemic countries. For controlled substances, carry original prescriptions and a note explaining medical necessity.
medications.generalAdvice: Tanzania has strict drug laws — penalties for possession or supply of any illegal drugs, including cannabis, include lengthy prison sentences, even for small amounts or transit passengers. Carry all prescription medications in original packaging with a doctor's letter. Medical facilities are limited outside Dar es Salaam, so bring adequate supplies of any essential medications for your entire trip.

scams.name: Kilimanjaro Unlicensed Guides
scams.description: Budget operators use unlicensed porters with inadequate safety equipment.
scams.avoidance: Use KINAPA-licensed operators. Verify porter wages and safety equipment.

scams.name: Zanzibar Spice Tour Ripoff
scams.description: Unofficial guides charge premium rates for brief visits, then pressure overpriced product purchases.
scams.avoidance: Book through your hotel or registered operators. Agree on pricing beforehand.

scams.name: Safari Bait and Switch
scams.description: Cheap safari packages substitute inferior vehicles or skip planned parks.
scams.avoidance: Get detailed written itineraries. Book with TATO-registered operators.

connectivity.simOptions: Vodacom or Airtel prepaid SIMs at Julius Nyerere Airport or any phone shop. Need passport. Very cheap data plans.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi at most hotels and lodges. Limited in safari camps and national parks. Zanzibar towns have decent connectivity.
connectivity.bestOption: Vodacom prepaid SIM for best coverage including safari areas. Buy at airport. Don't rely on WiFi during safari.

cultural.tipping: 10% at restaurants. Safari guides: $15-25/day per person. Kilimanjaro porters: $8-15/day. Hotel porters: TZS 2000-5000.
cultural.dressCode: Modest dress, especially on Zanzibar (Muslim culture) — cover shoulders and knees. Safari: neutral colors (khaki, olive, brown). Avoid blue/black (attracts tsetse flies).
cultural.greetings: 'Jambo' (hello) or 'Habari' (how are you) — response is 'Nzuri' (fine). Handshake is common. Elders are addressed with respect.
taboos: Photographing people without permission (especially Maasai — tip expected)
cultural.haggling: Expected at markets, souvenir shops, and with taxi/tuk-tuk drivers. Not at restaurants or supermarkets. Start at 30-50% of asking price.

safety.lgbtSafety: Tanzania is extremely unsafe for LGBTQ+ travelers. Same-sex relations are criminalized with penalties of up to 30 years imprisonment. There have been crackdowns and arrests. LGBTQ+ travelers must exercise extreme discretion and avoid any public displays of affection.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Solo female travel is possible but requires significant planning. Stick to established safari operators and tourist areas like Zanzibar, Arusha, and national parks. Dress conservatively, especially on the coast and Zanzibar (predominantly Muslim). Avoid walking alone at night.
safety.notes: Tanzania is a major safari and beach tourism destination with well-developed tourist infrastructure in key areas. Petty crime is common in Dar es Salaam and Arusha — don't walk with valuables. Safari parks and Zanzibar resort areas are generally safe. Use reputable tour operators and avoid walking alone at night in cities.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: visa on arrival ($50) or e-Visa. UK, EU, most nationalities eligible for visa on arrival.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: June-October (dry season, best for safari and Kilimanjaro). January-February (short dry season, calving in Serengeti). Avoid March-May (heavy rains).

steps: File a police report immediately — get the report number, you will need it
Contact the US Embassy or nearest consulate: Contact the nearest US Embassy
Bring the police report + any ID you have (driver's license, copy of passport)
Apply for an Emergency Passport (usually issued within 1-2 business days)
Notify your travel insurance and airline of the situation
stolenPassport.notes: Keep a digital copy of your passport in cloud storage (Google Photos, iCloud) and email yourself a scan before travel.

steps: Go to the nearest police station (or call 112)
Bring ID or a copy of your passport if available
Request a written report — ask for an English copy or certified translation if needed
Keep the report number safe — required for insurance claims
For theft: list all stolen items with approximate values
policeReport.notes: In many countries, tourist police stations are available in major cities — they have English-speaking staff. Ask your hotel concierge for the nearest tourist police.

steps: If involved in an accident: do not move vehicles if anyone is injured
Call police (112) and ambulance (114) if there are injuries
Exchange contact, license, and insurance details with other parties
Document the scene with photos before moving vehicles
Contact your rental car company's emergency line
Contact your travel insurance's 24h assistance line
roadsideAssistance.notes: Traffic drives on the LEFT. An International Driving Permit (IDP) is required for most foreign licenses. Rental vehicles are available at major airports and cities.

immediate: Move to higher ground during heavy rain
Do not cross flooded roads or streams
Follow Tanzania Red Cross and local authority guidance
after: Boil or purify drinking water after flooding
Avoid contact with floodwater — cholera and leptospirosis risk
Seek medical attention promptly if showing signs of waterborne illness
